thalidomide.definition: A sleeping pill sold from the late 1950s and given for morning sickness. Taken early in pregnancy, it caused severe birth defects in more than 10,000 children.

teratogen.definition: A substance that can harm an unborn baby while its body is forming, causing birth defects.

kefauver-harris-amendments.definition: A US law of 10 October 1962. Since then, a company must show with well-controlled studies that a new medicine works, not only that it is safe, before it may be sold.

substantial-evidence.definition: The proof US law asks for before a new medicine is approved: evidence from adequate and well-controlled studies that it does what its label claims.

adequate-and-well-controlled-study.definition: A study built to separate the effect of a medicine from chance, the natural course of the illness, the placebo effect and biased observation. It compares with a control group and usually uses randomisation and blinding.

drug-lag.definition: The delay before a new medicine becomes available in one country compared with others, or its absence there. Strict or slow approval rules are one possible cause.

conditional-marketing-authorisation.definition: An EU licence for a medicine that meets an unmet need, granted on less complete data. It lasts one year at a time, and the company must deliver the missing studies.

exceptional-circumstances-authorisation.definition: An EU licence for a medicine whose full benefits and risks cannot be shown, for example because the disease is very rare. The regulator reviews it every year.

accelerated-approval.definition: A US route, formalised in 1992, that approves a medicine for a serious disease on an early sign of benefit, such as a shrinking tumour. Later trials must confirm a real benefit.

accelerated-assessment.definition: A faster EU review, of up to 150 days instead of 210, for medicines of major interest to public health.

prime-scheme.definition: An EU programme, started in 2016, in which the European Medicines Agency gives early advice to developers of medicines for unmet needs, to speed up their development and review.

confirmatory-trial.definition: A trial done after an early approval to check that a medicine really helps patients, for example that they live longer.

orphan-medicine.definition: A medicine for a rare disease. Special laws in the US (since 1983) and the EU (since 2000) encourage companies to develop them.

user-fee.definition: Fees that companies pay the US FDA when they apply for approval. Since 1992 they pay for extra reviewers, in return for goals for how fast reviews are done.

directive-65-65.definition: The first medicines law of the European Economic Community, of 26 January 1965. It said no ready-made medicine may be sold without a licence based on test results. Directive 2001/83/EC replaced it.

wet-op-de-geneesmiddelenvoorziening.definition: The Dutch medicines law of 1958. It set up a board that registered packaged medicines. The Geneesmiddelenwet replaced it on 1 July 2007.

oxytocin.definition: A short peptide hormone. It makes the womb contract during birth and helps release breast milk. In 1953 it was the first peptide hormone made in a laboratory.

exendin-4.definition: A peptide first found in the venom of the Gila monster, a lizard. It switches on the same receptor as the human hormone GLP-1. The medicine exenatide is a lab-made version.

radioimmunoassay.definition: A lab test that uses antibodies and a radioactive label to measure very small amounts of a hormone in the blood.
